newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Battle looms for Russia chocolate market - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Battle looms for Russia chocolate market - analysts.

text.p: Russians are unlikely to rush to the shops to stock up on home-made chocolate despite an appeal by President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday to buy Russian goods, industry analysts said.

Confectionery industry sources and cocoa analysts said Russia's appetite for chocolate had stabilised after collapsing earlier in the decade, and that consumption of cocoa and its products was unlikely change much in the medium term.

"Russian cocoa consumption will not be much higher this year than last year, and I think cocoa imports will be about the same level as last year," said Alexander Pavlov, head of the Agriculture Ministry's confectionery industry department.
But analysts said that Yeltsin's Buy Russian remarks showed that the battle was on to win market share.
"Looking at the Russian chocolate confectionery market as a whole, I see it as growing steadily," said a representative at a Western confectionery company with operations in Russia.
"The key question is, who is getting this market?"
Yeltsin said Russia could hold its own in the face of stiff competition from abroad.
"Is Russian chocolate worse than imported chocolate? No, it's better," he said in a radio address.
Domestic chocolate manufacturers have had to battle against a rising influx of brightly-packaged, often high-quality Western goods which have flooded supermarket shelves in recent years.

Chocolate-making giants Cadbury of Britain and Masterfoods of the United States advertise their goods regularly on Russian television - giving them an advantage most domestic manufacturers cannot afford.
Cadbury, Mars and Nestle of Switzerland all have investments in confectionery production in Russia.
Pavlov said domestic confectioners did not need Yeltsin to advertise their goods and that the overall quality of Russian chocolate US hard red w wheat was improving.
But the Western manufacturer said research indicated that more and more Russians were complaining about falling quality standards in domestic confectionery.
Russian chocolate makers welcomed Yeltsin's attempts to support them, but they said that the president made no declaration about concrete steps they needed in order to prosper.
"Yeltsin's statement was a very strong one," said Anatoly Daursky, president of Russia's biggest confectioner OAO Red October.
"But it would have been more powerful if the government had lifted customs duties on some key products."
He said the company paid a five percent duty on cocoa bean imports and a 25 percent duty on sugar imports.
"Our outlook is very good if the government supports us, but if it does not, small and medium-sized companies will be ruined," he said.

Russia imported 55,900 tonnes of cocoa beans in 1996, down slightly from 56,300 tonnes in 1995. In the first two months of this year cocoa imports slipped to 11,000 tonnes from 12,200 tonnes over the same year-ago period, official data shows.

Analysts said official cocoa bean imports did not give a full picture of Russian chocolate consumption trends because Western manufacturers operating in the country were importing more cocoa in the form of cocoa liquor and butter.

The London-based International Cocoa Organization said Russian consumption was 144,000 tonnes cocoa bean equivalent in 1994/95, the last year for which data was available. This was down slightly from 148,000 tonnes consumed in 1993/94.
"I don't think there will be a significant change in consumption over the next few years," said one Western analyst.

Analysts linked Russian consumption trends to the country's overall economic performance. The purchasing power of the average Russian would have to increase significantly before cocoa and cocoa-product offtake took off, they said.
"Demand is there, but nowadays not a lot of people will be putting chocolate products at the top of their shopping lists," a second analyst added.
